claim: Widespread eccDNA formation occurs in human sperms.
source: Here, we revealed widespread eccDNA formation in human sperms and mouse spermatogenesis.
evidence: Supported by Circle-seq data showing eccDNAs across the human genome in sperm samples

claim: Widespread eccDNA formation occurs during mouse spermatogenesis.
source: Here, we revealed widespread eccDNA formation in human sperms and mouse spermatogenesis.
evidence: Supported by Circle-seq data from different developmental stages of mouse germ cells

claim: Germline eccDNAs are derived from oligonucleosomal DNA fragmentation in cells likely undergoing cell death.
source: We noted that germline eccDNAs are derived from oligonucleosomal DNA fragmentation in cells likely undergoing cell death, providing a potential new way for quality assessment of human sperms.
evidence: Supported by periodic size distribution (~180 bp), nucleosome occupancy predictions, and ChIP-seq data showing association with histones

claim: Germline eccDNAs provide a potential new way for quality assessment of human sperms.
source: We noted that germline eccDNAs are derived from oligonucleosomal DNA fragmentation in cells likely undergoing cell death, providing a potential new way for quality assessment of human sperms.
evidence: Inferred from the association between eccDNA formation and cell death

claim: Small-sized eccDNAs are associated with euchromatin.
source: Interestingly, small-sized eccDNAs are associated with euchromatin, while large-sized ones are preferentially generated from heterochromatin.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data showing enrichment at H3K27ac-marked euchromatin regions

claim: Large-sized eccDNAs are preferentially generated from heterochromatin.
source: Interestingly, small-sized eccDNAs are associated with euchromatin, while large-sized ones are preferentially generated from heterochromatin.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data showing enrichment at H3K9me3-marked heterochromatin regions

claim: Sperm eccDNAs are barely associated with de novo germline deletions.
source: By comparing sperm eccDNAs with meiotic recombination hotspots and structural variations, we found that they are barely associated with de novo germline deletions.
evidence: Supported by comparison showing minimal overlap between eccDNAs and known genomic deletions

claim: Microhomology-mediated end joining is the major eccDNA biogenesis mechanism.
source: Empowered by our method, we provided strong evidence to show that microhomology-mediated end joining is the major eccDNA biogenesis mechanism.
evidence: Supported by detection of microhomologous sequences at eccDNA breakpoints and sequence motif analysis

claim: Extrachromosomal DNA (ecDNA) in cancerous cells is usually megabase long in average.
source: The one exclusively present in cancerous cells is usually referred to as extrachromosomal DNA (eccDNA), which is of megabase long in average and plays key roles in tumorigenesis (Wang et al., 2021b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2021b

claim: Extrachromosomal DNA (ecDNA) plays key roles in tumorigenesis.
source: The one exclusively present in cancerous cells is usually referred to as extrachromosomal DNA (eccDNA), which is of megabase long in average and plays key roles in tumorigenesis (Wang et al., 2021b).

claim: Nucleosome wrapping of DNA might contribute to the formation of small-sized eccDNAs.
source: Epigenomically, the overall higher GC content, the periodicities of dinucleotide, and eccDNA size convergently point to that nucleosome wrapping of DNA might contribute to the formation of small-sized eccDNAs (Shibata et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2021a), an intriguing starting point for mechanistic understanding of eccDNA origination.
evidence: Supported by citations to Shibata et al., 2012 and Wang et al., 2021a

claim: Direct evidence for coincident positioning of eccDNAs and nucleosomes is still lacking.
source: However, direct evidence for coincident positioning of eccDNAs and nucleosomes is still lacking, not to mention specific epigenetic marks on nucleosomes that are tightly associated with eccDNA formation.
evidence: Statement about the state of knowledge in the field

claim: EccDNAs are increased upon DNA damages.
source: EccDNAs are increased upon DNA damages (Møller et al., 2015; Paulsen et al., 2021), suggesting them as by-products of successive DNA repairs.
evidence: Supported by citations to Møller et al., 2015 and Paulsen et al., 2021

claim: EccDNA levels particularly depend on resection after double-strand DNA break (DSB) and repair by microhomology-mediated end joining (MMEJ).
source: Among diverse repair pathways, it was reported that eccDNA levels particularly depend on resection after double-strand DNA break (DSB) and repair by microhomology-mediated end joining (MMEJ) (Paulsen et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2021a).
evidence: Supported by citations to Paulsen et al., 2021 and Wang et al., 2021a

claim: Microhomology is found around eccDNA breakpoints.
source: In further support of the involvement of MMEJ, microhomology is found around eccDNA breakpoints (Lukaszewicz et al., 2021; Møller et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lukaszewicz et al., 2021 and Møller et al., 2015

claim: In all studies using short-read sequencing technologies, eccDNA breakpoints are mis-annotated if microhomologous sequences are present around due to their interference to precise breakpoint detection.
source: However, in all studies using short-read sequencing technologies, eccDNA breakpoints are mis-annotated if microhomologous sequences are present around due to their interference to precise breakpoint detection (see our main text; Dillon et al., 2015; Henriksen et al., 2022; Kumar et al., 2017; Lv et al., 2022; Mann et al., 2022; Møller et al., 2018; Møller et al., 2020; Paulsen et al., 2019; Prada-Luengo et al., 2019; Shibata et al., 2012; Sin et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2021a; Zhang et al., 2021), or the eccDNA identification does not depend on precise breakpoint detections at all (Møller et al., 2015; Mouakkad-Montoya et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations and analysis in the manuscript

claim: During meiosis, two spatially closed break sites catalyzed by SPO11 at recombination hotspots may release eccDNAs accompanied by de novo deletions on linear chromosomes.
source: During meiosis, two spatially closed break sites catalyzed by SPO11 at recombination hotspots may release eccDNAs accompanied by de novo deletions on linear chromosomes (Lukaszewicz et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lukaszewicz et al., 2021

claim: Germline microdeletions display similar sequence features with eccDNAs.
source: Consistently, germline microdeletions display similar sequence features with eccDNAs (Shibata et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shibata et al., 2012

claim: The creation of germline eccDNAs negatively correlate with meiotic recombination rates.
source: However, a recent study reported that the creation of germline eccDNAs negatively correlate with meiotic recombination rates (Henriksen et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Henriksen et al., 2022

claim: Only a small fraction of histones will survive from the histone-to-protamine transition in mature sperms.
source: Only a small fraction of histones will survive from the histone-to-protamine transition in mature sperms, allowing us to more specifically correlate eccDNA origination with histones.
evidence: Established knowledge about sperm biology

claim: Germline eccDNAs are likely formed by microhomology-mediated ligation of nucleosome-protected fragments.
source: We conclude that germline eccDNAs are likely formed by microhomology-mediated ligation of nucleosome-protected fragments and barely contribute to de novo genomic deletions at meiotic recombination hotspots.
evidence: Supported by data showing microhomology at breakpoints and association with nucleosomes

claim: Germline eccDNAs barely contribute to de novo genomic deletions at meiotic recombination hotspots.
source: We conclude that germline eccDNAs are likely formed by microhomology-mediated ligation of nucleosome-protected fragments and barely contribute to de novo genomic deletions at meiotic recombination hotspots.
evidence: Supported by data showing minimal overlap between eccDNAs and recombination hotspots

claim: High content of eccDNAs existed in sperms.
source: Because it was reported that high content of eccDNAs existed in sperms (Henriksen et al., 2022), we examined the genome-wide eccDNA landscape in two human sperm samples by Circle-seq (Møller et al., 2018; Møller et al., 2015; Møller et al., 2020; see 'Materials and methods') and indeed found that there were widespread eccDNAs across the human genome (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by citation to Henriksen et al., 2022 and confirmed by data in this study

claim: There were widespread eccDNAs across the human genome in sperm samples.
source: Because it was reported that high content of eccDNAs existed in sperms (Henriksen et al., 2022), we examined the genome-wide eccDNA landscape in two human sperm samples by Circle-seq (Møller et al., 2018; Møller et al., 2015; Møller et al., 2020; see 'Materials and methods') and indeed found that there were widespread eccDNAs across the human genome (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by Circle-seq data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A

claim: Spermatogonial stem cells develop into spermatocytes (SPA) via mitosis.
source: A series of cell divisions and morphological changes are involved in spermatogenesis, where spermatogonial stem cells develop into spermatocytes (SPA) via mitosis, and SPA then undergo meiosis to produce haploid round spermatids (RST), which will take a dramatic morphological change and chromatin compaction to produce elongated spermatids (EST) and finally matured sperms (Hess and Renato de Franca, 2008; ROOSEN-RUNGE, 1962).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hess and Renato de Franca, 2008 and ROOSEN-RUNGE, 1962

claim: SPA undergo meiosis to produce haploid round spermatids (RST).
source: A series of cell divisions and morphological changes are involved in spermatogenesis, where spermatogonial stem cells develop into spermatocytes (SPA) via mitosis, and SPA then undergo meiosis to produce haploid round spermatids (RST), which will take a dramatic morphological change and chromatin compaction to produce elongated spermatids (EST) and finally matured sperms (Hess and Renato de Franca, 2008; ROOSEN-RUNGE, 1962).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hess and Renato de Franca, 2008 and ROOSEN-RUNGE, 1962

claim: Round spermatids take a dramatic morphological change and chromatin compaction to produce elongated spermatids (EST) and finally matured sperms.

evidence: Supported by citations to Hess and Renato de Franca, 2008 and ROOSEN-RUNGE, 1962

claim: From ~1500 to ~180,000 high-confidence eccDNAs were identified in mouse spermatogenesis.
source: From ~1500 to ~180,000 high-confidence eccDNAs were identified, suggesting widespread circular DNA formation during mouse spermatogenesis (Figure 1B; see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1B

claim: The reproducible rate of eccDNAs with 50% reciprocal overlap between biological replicates was only ~2.4% in average.
source: The reproducible rate of eccDNAs with 50% reciprocal overlap between biological replicates was only ~2.4% in average, a level comparable to previous studies (Henriksen et al., 2022; Møller et al., 2018; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and comparison with previous studies

claim: The detected eccDNAs seemed not saturated.
source: As noted earlier (Møller et al., 2018), the detected eccDNAs seemed not saturated (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C; see 'Discussion' and 'Materials and methods'), which might underlie the observed low reproducibility.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and citation to Møller et al., 2018

claim: The within-group similarity of eccDNAs was marginally higher than the between-group similarity.
source: Nevertheless, principal component analysis suggested that the within-group similarity was marginally higher than the between-group similarity (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), allowing investigation of stage-specific eccDNA features during mouse spermatogenesis.
evidence: Supported by principal component analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D

claim: The natural size distribution of eccDNA is usually distorted in Circle-seq as smaller eccDNAs tend to be overrepresented in rolling circle amplification.
source: The natural size distribution of eccDNA is usually distorted in Circle-seq as smaller eccDNAs tend to be overrepresented in rolling circle amplification (Mohsen and Kool, 2016; Møller et al., 2018; Møller et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mohsen and Kool, 2016; Møller et al., 2018; and Møller et al., 2015

claim: The detected eccDNA population was dominated by small-sized eccDNAs, most of which were ~180 bp or ~360 bp long.
source: As expected, the detected eccDNA population was dominated by small-sized eccDNAs, most of which were ~180 bp or ~360 bp long (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by size distribution data shown in Figure 1C

claim: EccDNA size could occasionally reach to several kilobases and even tens of kilobases.
source: However, eccDNA size could occasionally reach to several kilobases and even tens of kilobases (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1D

claim: EccDNAs from different cell types were all enriched at gene-rich regions, especially 5′UTR.
source: Second, eccDNAs from different cell types were all enriched at gene-rich regions, especially 5′UTR (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1E), corroborating the reported association between eccDNA frequency and gene density in somatic cells (Dillon et al., 2015; Shibata et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, and citations to Dillon et al., 2015 and Shibata et al., 2012

claim: EccDNAs were highly associated with SINE but not LINE elements.
source: ccDNAs were also highly associated with SINE but not LINE elements (Figure 1F), and quantitative analysis revealed that eccDNA biogenesis was positively correlated with SINE density (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F), but negatively correlated with LINE density (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1F, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1G

claim: EccDNA biogenesis was positively correlated with SINE density.
source: ccDNAs were also highly associated with SINE but not LINE elements (Figure 1F), and quantitative analysis revealed that eccDNA biogenesis was positively correlated with SINE density (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F), but negatively correlated with LINE density (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F

claim: EccDNA biogenesis was negatively correlated with LINE density.
source: ccDNAs were also highly associated with SINE but not LINE elements (Figure 1F), and quantitative analysis revealed that eccDNA biogenesis was positively correlated with SINE density (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F), but negatively correlated with LINE density (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G

claim: SINE and LINE elements function to orchestrate chromosomes into gene-rich A compartment and gene-poor B compartment, respectively.
source: Given that SINE and LINE elements function to orchestrate chromosomes into gene-rich A compartment and gene-poor B compartment, respectively (Lu et al., 2021), the positive correlation between eccDNAs and SINE elements might further support that eccDNAs are overall highly associated with the gene-rich regions.
evidence: Supported by citation to Lu et al., 2021

claim: There is a strong association between eccDNAs and DNA transposons.
source: Interestingly, we also noticed a strong association between eccDNAs and DNA transposons (Figure 1F), suggesting that DNA transposons might get circularized rather than or in addition to reintegrated into the genome, an interesting possibility awaiting further investigations.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1F

claim: DNA transposons might get circularized rather than or in addition to reintegrated into the genome.
source: Interestingly, we also noticed a strong association between eccDNAs and DNA transposons (Figure 1F), suggesting that DNA transposons might get circularized rather than or in addition to reintegrated into the genome, an interesting possibility awaiting further investigations.
evidence: Inferred from the association between eccDNAs and DNA transposons

claim: Sperm cells had 97,372 eccDNAs detected in average.
source: Notably, sperm cells had 97,372 eccDNAs detected in average, a number significantly higher than those in SPA (15,246), RST (18,426), and EST (3591) cells (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1B

claim: SPA cells had 15,246 eccDNAs detected in average.

claim: EST cells had 3,591 eccDNAs detected in average.

claim: SPA cells did not show higher eccDNA numbers, suggesting that meiosis does not seem to contribute significantly to eccDNA biogenesis.
source: SPA cells did not show higher eccDNA numbers (Figure 1B), suggesting that meiosis does not seem to contribute significantly to eccDNA biogenesis.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that SPA cells (undergoing meiosis) do not have more eccDNAs than other cell types

claim: EccDNA species in sperm cells has higher complexity.
source: Since the same amount of eccDNAs (10 ng) was used for library construction and all samples were sequenced in comparable and sufficiently-deep depth, it suggests that eccDNA species in sperm cells has higher complexity.
evidence: Inferred from the higher number of detected eccDNAs despite using the same amount of starting material

claim: The higher starting cell number for sperm cells might account for the larger diversity of sperm eccDNA species.
source: However, the higher starting cell number for sperm cells might account for the larger diversity of sperm eccDNA species (see 'Discussion' and 'Materials and methods'); otherwise, it would be interesting to explore any specific features of sperm cells underlying the higher load of eccDNAs.
evidence: Speculation about possible explanation for higher eccDNA diversity in sperm

claim: Sperm-derived eccDNAs showed a multimodal distribution with a pronounced periodicity of ~180 bp.
source: In contrast to SPA, EST, and RST eccDNAs showing the unimodal distribution that was centered at ~180 bp, sperm-derived eccDNAs showed a multimodal distribution with a pronounced periodicity of ~180 bp (Figure 1C), which was readily seen in individual samples (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 3

claim: Each nucleosome consists of 147 bp DNA wrapping itself around a histone core.
source: Given that each nucleosome consists of 147 bp DNA wrapping itself around a histone core, the ~180-bp-long fragments likely corresponded to histone core region plus ~20–30 bp linker regions, as observed in apoptotic cells (Matassov et al., 2004).
evidence: Established knowledge about nucleosome structure

claim: The ~180-bp-long fragments likely corresponded to histone core region plus ~20–30 bp linker regions, as observed in apoptotic cells.
source: Given that each nucleosome consists of 147 bp DNA wrapping itself around a histone core, the ~180-bp-long fragments likely corresponded to histone core region plus ~20–30 bp linker regions, as observed in apoptotic cells (Matassov et al., 2004).
evidence: Inferred from nucleosome structure and supported by citation to Matassov et al., 2004

claim: The different modes of size distribution might be due to distinct nucleosome compositions and structures between sperm and other spermatogenic cells.
source: Although the identified eccDNAs in all spermatogenesis stages were likely related to nucleosomes, the different modes of size distribution might be due to distinct nucleosome compositions and structures between sperm and other spermatogenic cells.
evidence: Speculation based on observed differences in size distribution

claim: Only a small fraction of histones will be retained in mouse sperm cells after histone-to-protamine transition.
source: Only a small fraction of histones will be retained in mouse sperm cells after histone-to-protamine transition (Torres-Flores and Hernández-Hernández, 2020), permitting us to more specifically correlate eccDNAs with histones.
evidence: Supported by citation to Torres-Flores and Hernández-Hernández, 2020

claim: Sperm eccDNAs had higher GC content than surrounding regions as well as control regions randomly selected across the genome.
source: We noted that sperm eccDNAs had higher GC content than surrounding regions as well as control regions randomly selected across the genome (Figure 2A), resembling the sequence feature of nucleosome-protected DNA fragments.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2A

claim: Sequence-based prediction revealed significantly higher nucleosome occupancy probability for ~180 bp and ~360 bp sperm eccDNA regions.
source: Consistently, sequence-based prediction revealed significantly higher nucleosome occupancy probability for ~180 bp (from 175 bp to 185 bp) and ~360 bp (from 355 bp to 365 bp) sperm eccDNA regions (Figure 2B; see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: Supported by nucleosome occupancy predictions shown in Figure 2B

claim: A small dip was observed at the center of ~360 bp eccDNA regions, which likely corresponded to the linker region between two nucleosomes.
source: A small dip was observed at the center of ~360 bp eccDNA regions, which likely corresponded to the linker region between two nucleosomes (Figure 2B, right).
evidence: Inferred from the observed pattern in Figure 2B

claim: 7.46% of sperm eccDNAs in total were intersected with at least one ChIP-seq peaks.
source: Taking advantage of public ChIP-seq data for histones and their modifications in mouse sperm cells (Jung et al., 2019; Jung et al., 2017; Singh and Parte, 2021), we found that eccDNAs were significantly enriched with certain histone variants and modifications (Figure 2C), and 7.46% of sperm eccDNAs in total were intersected with at least one ChIP-seq peaks.
evidence: Supported by analysis of ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 2C

claim: Enrichment of H3 histone and H2A.Z, TH2A, and TH2B histone variants but depletion of H3.3 variant was observed at ~180 bp sperm eccDNA regions.
source: Interestingly, enrichment of H3 histone and H2A.Z, TH2A, and TH2B histone variants but depletion of H3.3 variant was observed at ~180 bp sperm eccDNA regions (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq signal analysis shown in Figure 2D

claim: ~180 bp eccDNAs showed strong associations with H3K27ac, H3K4me1, H3K9ac, and H3K27me3 modifications.
source: These eccDNAs also showed strong associations with H3K27ac, H3K4me1, H3K9ac, and H3K27me3 modifications; however, no enrichment was seen for H3K4me3, and H3K36me3 and H3K9me3 signals were comparable with or even lower than randomly selected regions as control (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq signal analysis shown in Figure 2D

claim: No enrichment was seen for H3K4me3 at ~180 bp eccDNA regions.
source: These eccDNAs also showed strong associations with H3K27ac, H3K4me1, H3K9ac, and H3K27me3 modifications; however, no enrichment was seen for H3K4me3, and H3K36me3 and H3K9me3 signals were comparable with or even lower than randomly selected regions as control (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq signal analysis shown in Figure 2D

claim: H3K36me3 and H3K9me3 signals at ~180 bp eccDNA regions were comparable with or even lower than randomly selected regions as control.
source: These eccDNAs also showed strong associations with H3K27ac, H3K4me1, H3K9ac, and H3K27me3 modifications; however, no enrichment was seen for H3K4me3, and H3K36me3 and H3K9me3 signals were comparable with or even lower than randomly selected regions as control (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq signal analysis shown in Figure 2D

claim: Centers of ~360 bp eccDNAs were well positioned between two adjacent nucleosomes consisting of H3 histone and H2A.Z histone variants, and H3K27ac, H3K4me1, H3K9ac, and H3K27me3 histone modifications.
source: We next examined ~360 bp sperm eccDNAs, which supposedly correspond to two nucleosomes and made similar observations. Centers of ~360 bp eccDNAs were well positioned between two adjacent nucleosomes consisting of H3 histone and H2A.Z histone variants, and H3K27ac, H3K4me1, H3K9ac, and H3K27me3 histone modifications (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq signal analysis shown in Figure 2E

claim: ~360 bp eccDNAs did not show association with H3.3 or H3K4me3.
source: Similar to ~180 bp eccDNAs, ~360 bp eccDNAs did not show association with H3.3 or H3K4me3, or stronger association than randomly selected regions with H3K36me3 and H3K9me3 either (Figure 2E).
